utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The appearances for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Counsel. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis, Ekkehard Withopf, and Ruth Karper, the case manager.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Amir Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Chamber bids good morning to all the parties present, the OTP, the Defence counsel, the accused, as well as all the staff of this courtroom. This procedure of appearances is repeated every day; however, it is designed for the public, as the proceedings are broadcast, if anyone is following, it is important that the people present should be identified. That is why I'm asking you every time to introduce ourselves for the benefit of the public. Today we have a new witness, and I'm going to ask Madam Usher to go and bring the witness -- however, first let us hear Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Madam Judge, good morning, Your Honours. The Defence would like to tender the military maps that we discussed for the purpose of identification. We told to you -- we told you that these are maps that can be used by all the parties, the Prosecution and the Defence and Your Honours, and there are four different formats of these maps. And with your permission, I should like to begin with these maps in the scale of 1 to 200.000.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please don't disappear. Mr. Bourgon needs you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Would you be kind enough to distribute the following documents which explains the sources of the maps and also describes the region shown on each of these maps. For the purpose of identification, we would like to underline that these are military maps provided to us by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. These are maps that were used at the time by the Army of Yugoslavia. The series that we have are in the scale of 1 to 200.000. And the document with the Banja Luka indication on it was copied on one of these four maps. And on these documents, you have the four maps shown, that is, Banja Luka 4517; Doboj, 4518; Jajce, 4417; and Sarajevo, 4418. This is a document that illustrates the various maps, and I have a series of these maps, one for the Chamber, one for the registry, one for the Prosecution, and one set that we will be sharing, that is, both Defence teams will be sharing. In each of these tubes we have indicated the scale as well as the number of the maps, and for whom the maps are intended. The selection of maps was made to indicate the geographic areas mentioned in the indictment and the areas which the Defence will be using, both during the Prosecution case and during the Defence case. We have four maps, and the scale is 1 to 200.000. And as we go down to a lower scale, which means a more detailed presentation, it will be the same sector but a more particular area where certain acts may have been committed. Mr. President, the best procedure would be to give one number as identification for a whole series.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf, the Defence is providing us with four maps for the moment with a scale 1 to 200.000 covering the areas of Banja Luka, Doboj, Jajce, and the fourth region is Sarajevo. These maps, according to what the Defence tells us, are maps that were in force during the time of the JNA, as these were maps that were used by the army of the former Yugoslavia, and these maps precede the events that the Chamber is addressing. These were not maps drafted after but before the events. So does the Prosecution have any objections regarding the use of these maps, which could have been also been tendered by the Prosecution, if it had made such a request to the Army of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, there's no objection by the Prosecution to use and to tender these maps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Withopf. So let us give an exhibit number, as this will be simpler. So, Mr. Registrar, we have four maps which merit having a name and a number, Banja Luka, Doboj, Sarajevo, and Jajce.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let us first give an exhibit number for the introductory documents. So we will have one exhibit number for the three documents, TK200, set number 2; and the third document. So one exhibit number for these three documents.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhibit number will be DH74 for the B/C/S documents and DH74/E for the English translation of the how-to-put-together-map sheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we have DH74 for the three pieces of paper, three documents as introduction. Now, let us have a DH number for Banja Luka, 4717; Doboj, 4518; and another one for Sarajevo and for Jajce. So let us have four numbers for these maps.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the map number 4517, Banja Luka, gets the exhibit number DH75; the map number 4417, Jajce, gets exhibit number DH76; the map number 4518, Doboj, gets the exhibit number 77; and the map number 4418, Sarajevo, gets the exhibit number DH78. I apologise, the exhibit number should not be 77 but Exhibit Number DH77 for the map of Doboj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. For the record, the four numbers indicated are the maps in the scale 1 to 200.000. I should also like to indicate to the Chamber that these maps were in use prior to the conflict, during the conflict, and are still in use today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, indeed. I indicated that they were designed prior to the conflict. But they were used during the conflict and they are still being used, which means that they are absolutely acceptable. But as the scale doesn't change, it is eternal, no reason to change the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The second series of maps is in the scale 1 to 100.000. And I would like to ask Madam Usher to distribute the introductory documents for these maps. And I would like again to underline that the choice of maps and the sector represented on those maps, in the scale 1 to 100.000, is within the territory covered by the maps in the scale of 1 to 200.000 and that these maps were chosen as a function of the area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps, with other zones of responsibility in the surroundings, regarding the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina 1993. This is a series of six maps, and we have a copy for the Chamber, a copy for the Prosecution, and a copy for the registrar. There are two documents in colour which are identical, prepared by the accused in two languages to avoid any confusion. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A small clarification, Mr. Bourgon. You are giving us a map of Vares, 475. This geographic area is subdivided into four sections, -1, -2, -3, -4. Whereas, in the document produced, there are six subsections. Why are there four on the one hand and six on the other?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The document entitled "Vares," 475, was photocopied from one of these maps, and the region which has a darker line around it is divided into six squares, called Jajce, Zenica, Vares, Livno, Konjic, and Sarajevo, and this corresponds to the document in colour with the six squares. And if you have a look at the document in colour, above that we have Banja Luka, 423; and Doboj, 425. So we can easily understand which map is being referred to when they are used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We still don't have the maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I provided three sets, one for the Prosecution, one for the registry, and one for the Chamber, and there's a label on them, so they must be there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apparently one of the tubes is missing. Ah, here it is. I'm sorry. Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, the Prosecution has no objection in using and tendering these maps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Registrar, please give me a number for the two documents Vares, with the subsection in English and B/C/S. So a document for these -- a number for these document, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhibit number will be DH79; and for the English translation, DH79/E.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And now for the six maps in the scale 1 to 100.000.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the map number 473 for Jajce gets the exhibit number DH80; the map number 523, Livno, gets the exhibit number DH81; the map number 474, Zenica, gets the exhibit number DH82; the map number 524, Konjic, gets Exhibit Number DH83; the map 475, Vares, gets the exhibit number DH84; and the map number 525, Sarajevo, gets the exhibit number DH85.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Has everyone noted carefully the numbers, I hope? Having specified that we have given DH numbers to these maps, but we could also have given a DHK indication, because these are maps for both Defence teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, submitted on behalf of the two accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Are there any more maps?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next series of maps is in the scale 1 to 50.000, and we will use the same procedure. We have three documents. It's a series of eight maps. Mr. President, as we are going from the scale of 1 to 100.000 to the scale of 1 to 50.000, it is worth mentioning that the map is twice as precise because the area represented is twice the size of the map in the scale of 1 to 100.000. We have Zenica-4. It's a reproduction, a photocopy, of one of the maps, that is, the map Zenica-4, which you see indicated with a darker line on this document. So you see Zenica-4 as well as the areas represented by the eight maps we are tendering. So there's Zenica-1, -2, -3, and -4, and on the left-hand side there's Jajce-4, and then Livno-2, and Konjic-1, as well as to the right we see Vares-3. You can also see in the introductory documents that the other maps could also be presented to or shown to the Chamber if the parties find it fit to refer to a more detailed presentation of the area in presenting their case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Registrar, let us have a number for these two documents, Zenica-4, and six subsections.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhibit number will be DH86; and the English translation gets the exhibit number DH86/E.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we have eight maps, Zenica-1, -2, -3, -4; plus Jajce-4; Vares-3; Livno-2; and Konjic-1. So we have six maps. Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Again, Mr. President, Your Honours, no objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. President, there are eight maps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see, eight. One, two, three, four -- yes, exactly, eight maps. Eight maps.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the map Zenica-1 gets the exhibit number DH87; the map Zenica-2 gets the exhibit number DH88; map Zenica-3 gets exhibit number DH89; the map Zenica-4 gets the exhibit number DH90; the map Jajce-4 gets exhibit number DH91; the map DH -- the map Vares-3 gets the exhibit number DH92; the map Livno-2 gets the exhibit number DH93; and the map Konjic-1 gets Exhibit Number DH94.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Let us continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We have a last series of maps in the scale of 1 to 25.000 for the territories illustrated. They are again twice as large or more detailed than the previous one. So this is a series of 12 maps in the scale 1 to 25.000 which are presented similarly. It was not possible to use the same method as before. We just have a coloured document indicating each of the maps as they are represented and how they should be assembled should one wish to put them one next to the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, a number, please, for the B/C/S version and the English version.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhibit number is DH95 for the B/C/S version and DH95/E for the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We just have the tubes left now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This series in the scale 1 to 25.000 consists of 12 maps with the numbers as indicated on the document DH95. I should like to note for the benefit of the Chamber that on the tubes the series 200.000 bears the number 2; the series of 1 to 100.000 bears the number 3; the series in 1 to 50.000 bears the number 4; and the series in the scale 1 to 25.000 bears the number 5. So map number 1, in scale 1 to 500.000, we hope we will not need. Should the Chamber wish to have that map, which covers all the territories referred to in the indictment, the Defence may also provide that map.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we note that on the tubes we have the numbers 2, 3, 4, 5. Number 1 is missing because number 1 corresponds to a map in the scale 1 to 500.000. So we have 12 maps in the scale 1 to 25.000. Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, again, no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could we have a number for each map.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the map Livno 2-2 gets exhibit number DH96; the map Jajce 4-4 gets exhibit number DH97; the map Zenica 1-4 gets the exhibit number DH98; the map Zenica 2-3 gets the exhibit number DH99; the map Zenica 3-1 gets the exhibit number DH100; the map DH -- sorry, the map Zenica 3-2 gets the exhibit number DH101; the map Zenica 3-3 gets the exhibit number DH102; the map Zenica 4-1 get it is exhibit number DH103; the map Zenica 4-2 gets the exhibit number DH104; the map Zenica 4-4 gets the exhibit number DH105; the map Vares 3-1 gets exhibit number DH106; and the map Vares 3-3 gets the exhibit number DH107.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. All the maps have been tendered into evidence and they have been given definitive, final, exhibit numbers. When either of the parties needs one of these maps, it's sufficient to refer to the number. We will then produce the map in question. Madam Usher, could you call the witness into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir. Are you receiving the interpretation of what I am saying?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I am. Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you have been called here as a witness for the Prosecution, you have to make the solemn declaration. But before you do so, before you read out the text before you, it's necessary for you to inform the Trial Chamber of your identity. Could you please tell me your first and last names.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Launcelot James Cameron Kiggell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your date of birth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: 19th of February, 1966.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And which town or village were you born in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in Lincoln.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Which country is Lincoln in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the United Kingdom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your current profession?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am currently a teacher of economics and business studies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993, what was your official position at the time, ten years ago?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a British Army officer, and I was at the rank of captain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Have you already -- have you already testified before a court, or is this the first time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you will be testifying, you have to make the solemn declaration. Could you read the text that you have in your hands.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You may sit down. In the course of your exchanges with the Prosecution, the Prosecution probably told you how we would be proceeding. The Trial Chamber must also provide you with some information. You are a witness for the Prosecution. The Prosecution will be asking you some questions about events that you were an eyewitness of or perhaps an oral witness. The Prosecution is to your right. The person who will be asking you some questions is Mr. Withopf. He will be conducting his examination-in-chief, and after he has concluded the examination-in-chief, you will be cross-examined by the Defence. They are to your left. And the accused, who won't be speaking, are behind them. The three Judges, sitting before you, have the right to ask you questions at any point in time, either questions that are directly related to questions put to you by either of the parties, or they might ask you any other questions that might be of interest for the pursuit of justice. Before answering a question, think about your answer. If there is a question that you don't understand, ask the person putting it to you to rephrase it to ensure that your answer is clear. The proceedings here are oral. We don't have any written record, so we don't know what you will be saying. What you say will help to establish the truth. This is why it is necessary for your answers to be precise, clear, and concise. In addition, I have to remind you of two other factors: Firstly, you have made the solemn declaration, which means that you will tell the truth. If a witness lies, gives false testimony, the witness could be prosecuted for having given false testimony. This is the case in all countries. This is a measure I had to remind you of. Giving false testimony can be penalised. You could be given a fine or a prison sentence. In addition, there is another provision, but this shouldn't be applicable to you: If a witness answers a question and the information he provides might incriminate him, you have the right to refuse to answer the question. Nevertheless, the Chamber could compel you to answer the question. But if that is the case, the information you provide can't be used against you. So you have such immunity. So roughly speaking, this is how your testimony will proceed -- this is how the testimony of witnesses proceeds, so when a witness is called by the Prosecution, by the Defence, or by the Chamber. So without wasting any more time, the Prosecution may take the floor. Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Sir, you informed the Trial Chamber that in 1993 you've been a British Army officer. Can you please for the benefit of the Trial Chamber briefly summarise your military career within the British Army.

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: I joined the army in 1987 and was commissioned to officer in 1988. I then joined my unit. One of my first jobs was clearing up at Lockerbie. I spent a year commanding a platoon of 36 men and then in 1990 was sent on an operational tour to Northern Ireland, where I again commanded 36 soldiers. Then, came back and was selected to run and set up a team for specialist recruiting, running an event training. Came back and then rejoined the battalion, ready for another operational tour in Northern Ireland. And then after Northern Ireland, I was sent on my promotion to major's course, which was about six months long. I completed that and then rejoined my battalion in January 1993, where we were then told we were going to Bosnia in April that year. After doing Bosnia, I was then promoted to operations officer and I finished my military career at the end of December 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Sir, what was your military rank when you left the British Army?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: I was a captain.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you briefly, sir, inform the Trial Chamber what you've done after you left the British Army.

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: I then joined a commercial company that made water purification equipment. I worked for them for several years and then went and did a masters degree in business administration at Durham University. And the company invited me back to become a director, which I joined. And then last year in July, I left them to start my new teaching job.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Whilst being with the British Army, sir, did there come a time when you were deployed in the area of the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes. I was deployed in April 1993, and I stayed there until November 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please inform the Trial Chamber where you were deployed in the area of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: I was deployed in Central Bosnia. We were stationed in Vitez. And I worked there from May to the end of August. And then for the last two months I was deployed to Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Sir, what was the context of you having been deployed in the area of Central Bosnia you just described?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: The British Battalion were requested to work under UNPROFOR to help deliver aid and medical supplies in Central Bosnia and in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please also inform, sir, the Trial Chamber about the name of the military unit you formed part of during that period of time.

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: We were known as BritBat, which was short for British Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Whilst you were deployed in the area of Central Bosnia you just described, what was your responsibility? What duties were assigned to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: I was assigned to be a liaison officer for Zenica. And in my role, I was to find out information, what was going on in the area, which enabled the British Battalion to operate in Central Bosnia. This was so we could find out where it would be possible to deliver aid, medical supplies, and help where required.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: In fulfilling your duties as a liaison officer, what did you actually do? Can you please describe for the benefit of the Trial Chamber the daily routine.

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: I would leave Vitez and drive into Zenica and would often go into 3 Corps and other -- and just find out information that was going on in Zenica, other military units, just to get to know them, get to know the names of the commanders, also to speak to the international aid organisations, also to speak to some of the civil power as well, just to see what's happening and where the British Battalion could help at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please, sir, go into some more detail in respect to with whom you communicated whilst you were the liaison officer for the area of Zenica.

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Well, we liaised on the military side with 3 Corps. And we then also dealt with all the brigade commanders. So we had dealt with the 3 Corps commander, the deputy commander was also assigned a liaison officer within 3 Corps. So I used to deal with them regularly. And then as well as going round to the different brigades to speak to the commanders and other civil people.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What sort of civil people did you talk to?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: I spoke to the chief of the police. I spoke to the mayor, and also the ordinary civilians on the streets as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Prior to arriving in Central Bosnia, did you get any briefing from the British Army about the situation in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: We had many briefings before we deployed from Germany. We had briefings of what was going on. We had training to prepare us for the role. And then when we arrived in country, we then had a more up-to-date briefing of what had been happening in the war at that stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Briefings were given to you in respect to what was going on in the area. Can you please be a bit more concrete in that respect.

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes. When we arrived in Split, we were given a military briefing of what was happening on the war of that front, where the movements were, what was happening, and what we could, you know, expect, and what was perhaps predicted might occur.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please inform the Trial Chamber about the area you were deployed after you were assigned being the liaison officer with the 3rd Corps, with the ABiH 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: I was responsible for Zenica town and the surrounding area. I didn't go all the way down into the Lasva Valley, so the immediate surrounding area of Zenica and Zenica itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: At the time you were deployed in Zenica and the surrounding areas of Zenica, did you also talk to representatives of other international organisations?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes. I worked with the United Nations, the UNHCR, the Red Cross, various aid organisations that were operating in the area at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You earlier on mentioned, sir, that you were based in Vitez. Where in Vitez exactly were you based?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: We were based in the old school, which I recall -- it's Nova Bila, I think it is, it was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please describe for the benefit of the Trial Chamber a typical day, a typical workday whilst you were assigned as the liaison officer for the Zenica area.

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Sometime between 8.00 and 9.00 in the morning I would drive across into Zenica, either using the mountain route or the bypass, and would go and speak to representatives of 3 Corps, military people. I was really on my own to go and find out what information you could gather at that time. So there was no sort of set routine. It was just driving around, seeing what I could see, see who I could speak to, and then return back to the British Battalion round about 5.00 ready for a 6.00 briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You earlier on mentioned, sir, that you were deployed as the liaison officer in the Zenica area and the surroundings from May to August 1993. Can you, if possible, please provide us with some more specific dates, if you do recall.

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes. I came back down from Tuzla round about the 21st of May, and then took over my duties a couple of days later as Zenica LO. And then it was until the 31st of August I remained Zenica LO, where I then handed over to another army officer from our battalion, who became the Zenica LO, and I became the Tuzla liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You just mentioned that each work day finished with the briefing at 6.00 p.m. Where did this briefing take place?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: This took place in the British Battalion headquarters in the old school.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: In the old school in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Who attended such daily briefings?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: All departmental heads, the liaison officers, having been round at the area. We would then feed back our information into the meeting. The commanding officer would be there, the intelligence officer would be there, so everybody who needed to know, who represented a department within the British Battalion, was represented.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Sir, who was the commanding officer at the time, your commanding officer?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Alastair Duncan.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And to whom did Lieutenant Colonel Alastair Duncan report to? What was his chain of command?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: He reported to Brigadier Searby, who was based in Split.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: In the course of such daily briefings at 6.00 p.m., can you please inform the Trial Chamber what has been reported and what has been discussed at such briefings.

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: We would all give information of what we had seen going on that day, who we'd met, what information we'd gathered, and try and give an assessment of what could likely happen in our area of responsibility. So everybody shared the information and the intelligence officer would compile this information later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The intelligence officer would compile such information later on. Did the compilation of such information, of the information result in any report in writing?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: The report that was produced was called the milinfosum, the military information summary.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What was the purpose, sir, to have such milinfosums?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: The purpose was to collate all the information and get a picture of what was happening in the region, and also to see what trends and what's likely to happen. And then that information was then fed up the British chain of command, so they had an idea of what was going on in the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You already partially earlier answered my next question. Who was supposed to read the milinfosum?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Well, everybody had access to it. Having had the information at the meeting verbally told, everyone had a picture. And if you got the opportunity, everyone could read the milinfosum. So therefore having read it in the battalion, it would then be fed up to the brigade headquarters in Split and the people responsible there would read it and it would also be fed back to the UK.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did you yourself get an opportunity to read the milinfosums?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes, frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The milinfosums, did they stay within the British Army, BritBat?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: I think they did. The information may have been shared amongst the international community. I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please describe for the benefit of the Trial Chamber what Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the contents of a typical milinfosum has been at the time.

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: It would often have a report of the activity, who had seen the activity and reported it. And they would often be a comment by -- made in the text which the intelligence officer would insert either from talking and debriefing the liaison officers or the relevant people who had reported that incident for it to be fed back up the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Sir, can such a milinfosum be described as a summary of the daily briefings, or was it more comprehensive?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: It was more comprehensive because there often wasn't time to give so much detail at the meeting. So therefore it was -- I used to come in and give information to the intelligence officer, which was more detailed information, who I'd met, which wasn't really relevant at the 6.00 meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did such milinfosums also contain an analytical portion?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes. It -- again, from the information that was on the sheets, you know, you could perhaps make an analysis of what was happening and what could happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Who was the person or what was the position of the person who was responsible for putting together the information in the milinfosums?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: He was a captain and he was the intelligence officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, sir, that the intelligence officer had a broad knowledge of the situation in the area?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes. He would have got a good knowledge from speaking to all the different parties.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You earlier on mentioned, sir, that you met with many people, amongst them with commanders within 3rd Corps. Whom actually did you meet?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Well, I met Enver Hadzihasanovic, who was the 3 Corps commander; and then I met his deputy commander, which was Merdan; and then I met the liaison officer who was assigned to me, it was a chap called Edo, I can't remember his surname. And then I also met other individuals. Sakib, I think was the adjutant within 3 Corps and I also met other commanders at 3 Corps as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: How often did you meet the 3rd Corps commander at the time, Enver Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: I met them very regularly. At the beginning, it was almost daily. So I met them on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And to your recollection, sir, how often did you meet Dzemal Merdan?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Again, I met him on many occasions, either at 3 Corps or out on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What was Mr. Merdan's position at the time?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: He was the deputy commander of 3 Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: When you met Mr. Hadzihasanovic, where did you meet him?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: I met him at 3 Corps headquarters, which was based in the steelworks in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please describe for the benefit of the Trial Chamber how Mr. Hadzihasanovic's office looked like.

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: It was a large office. It had obviously been the chief executive's office of the steelworks. Over to the left you had his desk and there were some couches just to the left of that. And then you had a huge boardroom table to the right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: When you met Mr. Hadzihasanovic in his office, were there occasions when you've seen maps, military maps?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes, there were maps that had been spread out onto the table.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Were these military maps?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes, it would have pictures of military movements.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Where did Mr. Dzemal Merdan, the deputy commander, where did he have his office?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: He had a small office to the side on the right, and it had a connecting door into Hadzihasanovic's office.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: During the time you were deployed as the liaison officer for BritBat in Zenica, who was your main point of contact with the ABiH 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Initially it was Hadzihasanovic, but then I was assigned a liaison officer. So I would -- if I had sort of questions, I would ask the -- Edo, the liaison officer. But you know, this was interspersed with meetings with Hadzihasanovic and Merdan.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please explain to the Trial Chamber, sir, why a liaison officer, the person with the name Edo, was assigned to you?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: I understand from a conversation with Hadzihasanovic and Lieutenant Colonel Duncan that he complained I was finding out too much information and, therefore, he signed a liaison officer to me. So he was sort of replicating what the British Battalion were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Whilst you were assigned as the liaison officer, did you ever meet any other military unit commander of the ABiH 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes. I met several. I remember meeting Kubura. I can't remember the names of other commanders that I'd met, but I remember meeting Kubura.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Do you recall, sir, where you met Mr. Kubura?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: At 3 Corps headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What was Mr. Kubura's position at the time, to your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: He was the 7 Muslim Brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And where was the 7th Muslim Brigade headquarters?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: It was located in Zenica. And I think, again, it may have been located in an old school.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: How far was the 7th Muslim Brigade headquarters away from the 3rd Corps headquarters?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: It may have been a few miles, because it was on the other side of town, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did you make any attempts to meet Mr. Kubura at other occasions?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes. I tried on several occasions to go to 7 Muslim Brigade headquarters, but I was never allowed entry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please provide us some more detail in that respect.

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: I'd turned up at the entrance to 7 Muslim Brigade, and I asked the guard to see if I could organise a meeting, but I would never be allowed to proceed further than the gate, so I would have to turn around and carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Do you have any explanation why, as to why you were not allowed to access the area of the 7th Muslim Brigade headquarters?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: It may have been that they had received orders not to allow anyone from UNPROFOR in, and that could be one possible explanation. Or Kubura wasn't there. I just never seemed to be allowed in.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Coming back to the meetings with Mr. Hadzihasanovic. At whose request or at whose initiative did such meeting -- meetings take place?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Normally it would be through the British Battalion's initiative, either myself organising the meeting, calling to see if I could see him without having anything organised, or sometimes I would organise meetings with Hadzihasanovic and Lieutenant Colonel Duncan.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Whilst assigned between May and August in the area of Zenica, did you travel a lot?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes, I travelled all around the region of Zenica, all around the town, and then in the surrounding area as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Were you allowed to travel freely?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Generally, yes. However, when we used to come across some checkpoints, you know, we would be refused access. So therefore we'd have to go and get authority from 3 Corps to have access to proceed through that checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Was this a regular occurrence, that there were ABiH 3rd Corps checkpoints and you were not allowed to get access?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Quite often it happened; and therefore, it would delay the whole proceeding, because we would have to go and get the relevant piece of paper, to get permission. And then once we got permission, we'd come back to the checkpoint. And again, it still had to be confirmed by the brigade headquarters - excuse me - to get through the checkpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Had to be confirmed by the 3rd Corps headquarters. Who actually was in charge for issuing such permissions?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: It was normally Merdan who was the man I'd normally have to get the sign the piece of papers. Whoever had the authority, who they would expect to sign it, would then allow us to go on our way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Was the 3rd Corps commander, Hadzihasanovic, also involved?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes. I think we -- on several occasions we had to get his signature on a piece of paper to go through checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: After you were deployed in the area of Zenica, sir, did there come a time when you noticed foreigners in that area?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes. We met foreigners, apart from the international aid community, we met people who were Mujahedin, who'd travelled from Turkey and other Muslim countries to help fight for the Muslims in the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: These Mujahedin, were they armed?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes. They -- when they were out on the ground, they were generally well armed. They had automatic weapons, grenades and rocket-propelled grenades.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: When for the first time after you arrived in the area did you notice such well-armed Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: I first saw Mujahedin in Zenica at the end of May, I met them in a suburb of Zenica. They weren't armed at that stage, because I was just having a meeting within a cafe bar which I think they had taken over.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: These Mujahedin, did they wear military uniforms?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes, they generally wore a uniform. They had -- quite often had a shawl, which is from that region. And they also had sort of -- I suppose you could describe them as having a sort of -- a typical Muslim beard, had grown it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The uniforms they wore, did they display any military insignia?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes. They often they would have a badge on the shoulder to represent the unit they belonged to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Sir, with the permission of the Trial Chamber, I'm going to show you a photo board. It's Prosecution Exhibit P4. And we will use the Sanction technology. Sir, can you please have a look at the photo board in front of you. And can you inform -- please inform the Trial Chamber whether the Mujahedin you've seen in Zenica end of May 1993 wore or had any of the patches displayed on this photo board on their uniforms.

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Well, I remember seeing -- I couldn't say whether I'd seen the patches in May. But generally the patches you saw were number 9 and 15. I can't remember exactly if they had the patches on in May, but I certainly remember seeing Mujahedin with patches on during my time there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: When for the first time, if you do recall, when for the first time have you seen Mujahedin wearing the patches you just identified?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: I couldn't accurately give you a date or a time when I saw those patches on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. To your knowledge, sir, which military unit did the Mujahedin form part of?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Generally they -- they belonged to 7 Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Is the 7th Muslim Brigade the ABiH military unit Mr. Kubura was the commander of at the time?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: To your knowledge - and I know you already mentioned it partially earlier - to your knowledge, where did the Mujahedin come from? From which foreign countries?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Generally, they came from Middle Eastern countries. The ones I had met came from Turkey and Istanbul. There was one example of one report of a Mujahedin coming from the UK.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, with your permission, I'm going to show the witness milinfosum number 30, dated 29th of May, 1993. The necessary copies are available. They are available in B/C/S, in English, and for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, in French as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Sir, can you please have a look at the milinfosum in front of you. If I may draw your attention to paragraph 2 of this -- of this milinfosum, which has the heading "Zenica." The first sentence, sir, starts with: "The Zenica LO reports, the following personality details for Zenica-based BiH brigades." Is the Zenica LO referring to you?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Under 2(b), there is mentioned 7th Muslim Brigade commander Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes. That's the information I found out that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: If I may, sir, draw your attention to paragraph 3 of this milinfosum. It starts with "A recce C/S conducted an extensive tour of the current line of confrontation." Can you please for the benefit of the Trial Chamber explain to us what a "recce C/S," what does it mean?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: This is short for a reconnaissance call sign, a recce call sign. And they had obviously done a reconnaissance along the current line of confrontation between the BiH and HVO forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: If I may draw your attention, sir, to paragraph 3 and then in brackets (3). Can you please explain for the benefit of the Trial Chamber what "GR 184056," what does it mean.

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: That is grid reference 184056.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And can you please also for the benefit of the Trial Chamber explain for what purpose grid references are used for.

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: This is to accurately map where certain instances where -- or checkpoints where, you know, where people were.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Would you be able, sir, if I would show you a map, to identify this location which is identified by its grid reference on a map?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I'm now going to show the witness a map. Unfortunately, this map is not available in Sanction due to technical reasons, but we have the respective numbers of hard copies. Can the witness please put the map on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Sir, is it possible for you to identify on this map, using the grid reference in the milinfosum, the place, the location which is identified under 3(3) of the milinfosum?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes. I'm just looking for the grid lines so I can accurately give you the grid reference and point it to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Please take your time, sir.

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I apologise. I can find the northings but I can't find the eastings on this map.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Would you be able, sir, without using the grid reference -- references to roughly describe the area which this grid reference is making reference to?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: I'll have a look. It's to the area of -- I can see from the report it says Fazlici, which is 1805. Can you please, --

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please, sir, encircle the location called Fazlici.

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: It's -- well, from --

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can the witness please be provided with a text liner.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the Prosecution wishes to tender this map into evidence. If the witness could please date and sign the map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the Defence wishes to intervene. But I, too, would like you to explain how on the basis of the milinfosum, paragraph 3, how the witness is managing to locate the position. Maybe that will be the question of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, precisely so. We wanted to know what the witness has actually done. Has he read out from the map the name Fazlici referred in the milinfosum and encircled it, which could be done by anyone, especially as the witness in answer to previous questions from the Prosecutor said that he was throughout stationed in Zenica, that he only moved around the environs of Zenica, and that he was not assigned to tour the area beyond. So we do not see what the purpose of this marking is, because unlike the witness we heard before this witness, this witness has not provided a single piece of evidence that would qualify him to mark these areas. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Withopf, it would be desirable for the witness to explain to us how, on the basis of the fact that he has Fazlici 1805, how he has found the spot. Mr. Witness, could you explain to us technically how GR 1805 is found on this map. If Fazlici had not been indicated but GR 1805, would you be capable of pointing out the spot on the basis of the map -- on this map? First, what does the "GR" mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It means "grid reference," which therefore applies to the map. And the two figures -- the four numbers represent the square for that town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So "GR" refers to the grid reference, and the numbers to the squares; is that right? So theoretically one should be able to find "G" and "R" on the map.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: "GR" is the terminology to use. What you then look on the map are the actual numbers. And one of the difficulties when I was looking for number 3 was looking for the numbers going across the page which would accurately give me the location of where that checkpoint was. But I'd found "05" on the northing lines, so that pointed me to the right area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So 1805. And 18, is that a vertical line or a horizontal line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I could show you on your map, sir. These numbers here are known as northings, and you can see them going down that way. So 05 should be that box. And then the numbers I couldn't make out were the numbers going across the columns of the map, which I couldn't see. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may please assist the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: May I draw your attention, sir, to what's written under 3.A. and I understand you were actually earlier on referring to this portion of the milinfosum. It says "There are still the following checkpoints on the road between Stara Bila and Fazlici." And then after "Fazlici" there's a grid reference.

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: How does this grid reference after Fazlici, namely 1805, how does it correspond to the grid reference under (3), 184056?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: The grid reference 184056 is obviously very close to Fazlici and therefore we might be able to work out where this checkpoint is.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Does this information contained in the milinfosum, together with the map you have in front of you, allow you to identify the area which is mentioned under 3(3) of the milinfosum as being Fazlici?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, again, the Prosecution wishes to tender this map into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, this map, first of all, was already tendered by the Prosecution in a larger version at the very beginning. I think that it is Exhibit Number P1. That was the first exhibit tendered by the Prosecution. Today the witness is being used to recognise a town. If for the record the witness tells us that he saw Fazlici on the map because he saw the word "Fazlici" written, the Defence has no objection. If the witness is telling us that he recognises Fazlici on the basis of the grid references provided in the milinfosum, then the Defence has an objection because the witness is not capable with the map given him to identify the coordinates, the grid references. He can find 05, and everyone can see that on the map. The coordinates 05 doesn't even correspond to Fazlici. 058 may correspond to Fazlici but not 05. 05 corresponds to Orasac. Whereas, the other coordinates cannot be seen on this map, and the witness cannot tell us that grid reference 1805 corresponds to Fazlici.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you have heard the technical remarks made. When you encircled "Fazlici," did you do that because you saw in the milinfosum the name of Fazlici and you found it on the map, or is it basically exclusively on the basis of your technical knowledge, GR 1805, that you found Fazlici? As you have taken the solemn declaration, you will give me an answer telling the truth. What are you telling us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I found Fazlici by using the grid reference on the milinfosum.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think the witness has very clearly answered the questions and addressed the concern of the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The witness tells us that relying on his technical and military knowledge he was able to find Fazlici, so that's it. What can the Defence tell us? What do you wish to tell us?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I simply wish to confirm, Mr. President, that when the witness tells us that he uses the coordinates in the milinfosum, is he telling us that on the map in front of him that Fazlici corresponds to the grid reference 1805? If that is the case, we have no objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, witness, on the map, you are identifying Fazlici on the basis of grid reference 1805. You are telling us in the affirmative?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, before - and I would suggest we have a break within a few minutes - but can this map please be given a Prosecution exhibit number. I understand the Defence, after the explanations by the witness, have no further objections in tendering it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, could I just clarify one point, and that's whether --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Dixon, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I just want to clarify that at this stage the Prosecution is only seeking to exhibit the map and not the military information summary. Because we have some comments to make in respect of whether this witness is the correct witness through this which document could in fact be admitted. So if we could be given an opportunity to address Your Honours on that point. But the way I understand it is that at this stage only the map is being sought to be tendered.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, at this stage, only the map is sought being tendered. However, at a later stage obviously the Prosecution wishes to tender the milinfosum as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. For the moment, we are only being asked to admit the map. As it is time for the break, we will come back and tell you what we have decided about the map. And I invite everyone to be back here at five to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After having deliberated and after having carefully examined the map and the grid reference 1805, the Trial Chamber notes that in fact GR 1805, although it doesn't indicate this exact place, is just above it. So as a result, we will give the document in question a final exhibit number. Mr. Registrar, could we have an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhibit number will be P98.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Mr. Withopf, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President, Your Honours. Mr. President, Your Honours, as already foreshadowed prior to the break, the Prosecution wishes to also tender into evidence the milinfosum number 30, dated 29th of May, 1993. The witness is personally mentioned in this milinfosum as the Zenica liaison officer. He was at the time. The witness was able to comment on the statements that do form part of the milinfosum, and for that reason the Prosecution wishes to tender this milinfosum into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Defence may comment on this. Before they do so, I'd like to point out that this milinfosum document number 30 is dated the 29th of May, 1993. This date is part of the relevant period that appears in the indictment. This document refers to a liaison officer. We have this person in front of us. He is our witness. And it is also interesting to point out that yesterday the Defence requested that a document of this type be admitted into evidence. What does Mr. Dixon have to say about this matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. It is correct that we have asked for documents of this kind to be admitted, but we've done so on the basis that the witness was able to identify relevant information in the document or was associated with certain events in the document. In this particular military information summary, the witness, as he said in his testimony, was able to identify one part of it, that is, paragraph 2, where he reported that the commander of the 7th Brigade was Mr. Kubura. That's not a contentious point. But that is the only aspect of the document that he has anything to do with, in our submission. Paragraph 3, which is clearly the most important paragraph in the document which the Prosecution seeks to rely upon, was one which involved an incident where the witness was not present. This was as a result of a recce which was conducting a tour along a confrontation line. And the witness was not in the area at the time. He didn't gather this information. This information was gathered by other persons, persons who themselves could testify about these events before the Tribunal. And, Your Honours, in our submission this is very significant, because although the Prosecution doesn't emphasise the point, the only reason why they're seeking to introduce this paragraph, surely, is because of the presence of foreign fighters at a certain point. They are seeking to use this document to prove the truth of its contents, to prove that those persons were there at that time. This witness wasn't there at the time. He can't testify about whether or not this document is accurate. And the Defence are not in the position to be able to cross-examine him on that point. In addition, in his testimony earlier on, he indicated that these reports were drawn up by intelligence officers. So he wasn't the person drawing up the reports. They were put together by somebody else. He says he did look at some of these reports from time to time. This may well be one of the first times that the witness has seen this report or studied it in any detail. And in our submission, we don't have, therefore, the correct witness through which to introduce this document, which would provide the Defence with a proper opportunity to -- to cross-examine on the point of evidence, the presence of these fighters in a certain position at a certain time. He didn't draw up the report, and more importantly, he wasn't there at the critical time. And on that basis, we would ask Your Honours not to admit this document into evidence at this stage. It can be marked for -- for identification, as has been done with many other documents. And when the appropriate witness does arrive, then the matter could be reconsidered at that time. I'm grateful, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. General Hadzihasanovic's Defence counsel agrees with the arguments presented by Mr. Kubura's Defence. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, if I may please briefly respond. We are at the very similar, if not the say, the very same situation yesterday. And as Your Honour, the Presiding Judge, already pointed out, yesterday the Prosecution at no point in time did object to any of the milinfosums presented by the Defence being tendered, although in all such instances only very small portions of the milinfosum were the subject of any comments by the witness. This situation is exactly the very same as yesterday, when documents presented -- milinfosums presented by the Defence were tendered into evidence. I also wish to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber to the fact that the milinfosums are official documents, official documents of BritBat and official documents of UNPROFOR, an UN -- official UN organisation. The witness was able, Mr. President, Your Honours, to comment on contents of the milinfosum in question. The witness attended the regular 6.00 p.m. briefing meetings in Vitez in which such issues were discussed. And the witness himself was making reference to the fact that he has seen Mujahedin in Zenica and in the area surrounding Zenica. Therefore, the Prosecution is of the view that this document, this milinfosum, can be tendered into evidence and reiterates its request to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are there any other questions you would like to ask the witness about the document, or have you finished the questions you had about the document? Mr. Withopf, are there any other questions you wanted to ask about any other parts of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Just for clarification - and this may assist the Trial Chamber in its final determination - if I may ask the witness a question in respect to Mujahedin camps. With your permission, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But is this question one that relates to this document or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: It's not directly linked to this document, but it may assist the Trial Chamber in making its final determination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If that could help us to take an informed decision, please go ahead with your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Sir, during the time you were the liaison officer in Zenica and the area surrounding Zenica, did you become aware of Mujahedin running any camps in the area of Zenica or the surrounding area?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes. I was working with Norwegian's People Aid who were building a refugee camp to the east of Zenica and they reported they had problems with a Mujahedin training camp there and had asked for UNPROFOR assistance to see if it could settle this matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Were you present, sir, in the course of the regular 1800 hours' meetings, briefing meetings, in Vitez at times when the Mujahedin issue was raised and discussed during such meetings?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes, because I was sharing this information among with other departmental heads in the British Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: This additional information, Mr. President, Your Honours, may assist the Trial Chamber in making its determination, and the Prosecution reiterates its request to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. The Defence would like to say that the questions that have just been put to the witness don't -- won't enable the Trial Chamber to appreciate -- to assess the truth, the value of the document. And I think that all the issues -- all these issues have been raised by my colleague Mr. Dixon. If we want to tender this document to say that -- to show that it's a BritBat document, I don't think that the Defence objects to tendering the document as such. The problem is the contents of the document. The witness who is before the Trial Chamber today cannot provide any information that would allow the Trial Chamber to verify the truth of what is stated in paragraph 3. The Trial Chamber can take note of what is in paragraph 2. The witness has told us today that via the contact that he had he was aware of foreigners being present in the north of Zenica. If we have a look at the map, Mr. President, we're not at all referring to the same sector. We're not referring to the sector that the witness was referring to. Later on we are certain that the witness will talk about other meetings that he had, but what is mentioned in the milinfosum is the Fazlici area, and that is not an area that was a part of the area of responsibility of this witness. He says that he may have heard this being discussed at meetings held at 6.00. These subjects were discussed. But the fact that he heard about it is one thing; the fact that he doesn't know who he heard it about -- who he heard it is another matter. And today he cannot recall what is called the call sign in paragraph 3; that means the vehicle, the team, the patrol who made these observations. If the witness can say that yes, it's call sign 34 which accompanied the platoon, in such a case this could give additional weight to the probative value of the contents of the document. But how can we give any probative value at the moment to an affirmation, to a claim that is of great importance for our case. Given that the witness didn't observe the area, he didn't know who made these observations, perhaps the witness heard information about foreign soldiers. But for all these reasons, Mr. President, it's Rule 89(C) that should be respected by the Trial Chamber in this case; that is to say, it has to do with the probative value and the right for a fair trial that the accused have. How can we question this witness if he didn't see this himself and doesn't know who provided this information? And for these reasons, Mr. President, we think that if the Trial Chamber decides to admit this document they should take into account the comments made by the Defence. The only probative value of this document relates to the truth of paragraph 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Withopf, I'll let you take the floor in a minute. But first of all, Witness, when you had these meetings which took place at 6.00, how many of you were there? There was Lieutenant Colonel Duncan, the information officer, the liaison officer. How many of you were there at the table?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Approximately about 20 people perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, there were about 20 of you. And the patrols, did they have radio links with the command unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they would have radio links with the command unit, and the information would have been passed on when they came --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The unit which hasn't been identified which was on patrol and which saw Mujahedin in the place in question, did this unit report via radio, or was it the person in charge of the unit who was one of the 20 persons at the table?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I couldn't say how this was reported, whether it was from radio message or whether it was a face-to-face meeting with the intelligence officer. And therefore, it may not have been anyone at that meeting who was present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you discussed various issues at these meetings and you knew that there was a report that was going to be forwarded to your superiors, since these reports were intended for various superiors, did they sometimes fail to mention certain events in these reports if these events weren't sure? Did your colonel say, "Yes, you have informed me of this, but I'm not going to take this into account because it hasn't been verified, it's not certain"? Or did these reports contain everything that was said without any checks having been carried out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These reports were compiled by the people involved debriefing to the intelligence officer. So he would compile the information. At the meeting at 6.00, we were given an overview of the day's activities by the intelligence officer as a result of his meetings with the people who had seen events on the ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I have understood you correctly, it's the intelligence officer who would compile the report. He drafted the report. When you're mentioned as the liaison officer, did you make an oral report or a written one? If you made a written report, he would mention your report in -- in his report, or was there a record of the meeting which would state that you spoke to mention an event? How did these things happen? Did this intelligence officer compile a report on the basis of the written documents provided by other persons, or was it a document that was a record of the meeting that took place and which was attended by the 20 persons we have mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: These meetings I orally gave him the information, which he would then compile into the milinfosum. So he would take notes during our meeting to do an accurate report later on that evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're telling us that during the meeting with the intelligence officer -- what was his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: His name is Simon Harrison.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this intelligence officer would take notes. And then on the basis of these notes, he would compile his report. Very well. Mr. Withopf, we now have a better understanding of how this document was compiled. What do you have to say before we withdraw to deliberate briefly?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. President, Your Honours, the witness was able to provide additional information in favour -- in the view of the Prosecution, in favour of the Prosecution's request to tender this document into evidence. If I may briefly respond to my learned friend's submission. These are issues that have been discussed repeatedly. It appears to me that my learned friend from the Defence side is mixing up two issues. The one is the question of the admissibility of documents; and the other issue is the probative value of such a document. The probative value has nothing to do with the issue of admissibility of the document. And the second issue is the issue of hearsay. Hearsay, as this Trial Chamber has repeatedly ruled upon, is admissible, and the probative value will be determined later on in the course of these proceedings. Therefore, the Prosecution again reiterates its request to tender this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Bourgon, I'll let you take the floor for one last time, because this shouldn't turn into a ping-pong game. But we should point out, as the Prosecution has stated, two matters should be distinguished, admissibility of a document, which is based on the relevance of certain facts, and then the probative value of a document. And this is for the Trial Chamber to decide at a subsequent date. Mixing up these two matters can cause such problems. If a document is admitted, this doesn't mean that the contents of the document have probative value. The probative value of the document is for the Trial Chamber to decide on at a subsequent date. So I see that there's some confusion as to the distinction between admissibility and probative value. The probative value is a matter to be determined at a subsequent date once the Trial Chamber has all the information at its disposal. All the more so in that there will be other witnesses who will be appearing and who will be referring to certain matters mentioned in this document. That is certain. So I don't see why this document shouldn't be admitted at this stage. But we'll deliberate about this. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We agree with the Trial Chamber that there is a difference to be made between the admissibility of a document and the probative value that a document should be given.
