These are two entirely different matters, and the Defence is not confusing these matters. Nevertheless, there is a link between the two. This is referred to in Rule 89(C), which says that if the probative value is far lower than the relevance of the document and it could be detrimental to a fair trial, in such a case there is a relation between the two ideas. These are two different matters, but there is a link. And our argument today, Mr. President, is that the probative value that we might give a document that hasn't been established by the witness, and if the witness doesn't know who provided the information, all the witness can tell us about is how the document was compiled, well, that's one matter. But I'll go back to the first issue, Mr. President. Why does the Prosecution want to tender this document? Does it want to tender the document to show that it exists? We don't object to that. But is it to show that the contents are true? In such a case the Defence stands by its objection. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will withdraw. Don't move. We'll be back in a few minutes. --- Break taken at 11.27 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, the Trial Chamber has deliberated in order to decide whether this milinfosum number 30, dated the 29th of May, 1993 should be admitted into evidence. It is the opinion of the Trial Chamber that this document should be admitted. The Defence argued that with regard to the fact that it was stated there were Mujahedin in a certain place and that the witness didn't see this himself. The Trial Chamber takes note of the Defence's position, and the Trial Chamber will clarify this issue mentioned in the report. But the witness wasn't an eyewitness of this event. It's just based on hearsay. But that's not the only point referred to in the document. The witness himself has mentioned other events mentioned in paragraph 2, and as a result, as we did yesterday, we believe that this document can be admitted into evidence. We believe that Rule 89 has been respected, since the Defence in the course of its cross-examination can go back to the issue and ask the witness all the appropriate questions. So Mr. Registrar, could we have a number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the exhibit number will be P99.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] P99. Please continue, Mr. Withopf. Just a moment. The witness needs to sign and date this document. Witness, will you please put your name and today's date on this document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As there's a document translated into B/C/S, into French, and into English, we need numbers for all three language versions. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the B/C/S version gets the exhibit number P99/BCS; the French version gets the exhibit number P99/F.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Withopf, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Sir, a few minutes ago you already made reference to an issue related to Mujahedin and a location called Arnauti. Can you please provide the Trial Chamber with additional information on this issue.

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Sorry, I didn't catch that. Did you say please ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please tell us more about this issue related to Arnauti.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour, I don't wish to interrupt soon again, but the witness never gave a name for where a particular camp might have been situated.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that was my understanding. Mr. Withopf, when the witness answered the question put to him, did he mention this locality? I think not. But we need to check on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, if you allow me to briefly consult the transcript. Mr. President, Your Honours, it appears to be correct that the location which is known as Arnauti has not yet been mentioned by the witness, and I do apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Sir, were you yourself during the time you were the liaison officer between BritBat and the 3rd Corps, the ABiH 3rd Corps, were you involved in any issues related to Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: We got a call from the Norwegian's People Aid, who were based east of Zenica in the Arnauti area, where they were building a refugee camp. They had complained of a Mujahedin training area being located next to it. And they were coming across saying that this refugee camp shouldn't be built and they were planning to build a mosque. I had been called in, as this was in the -- my area of responsibility, to see if we could resolve the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And can you please also inform the Trial Chamber whether you were able to resolve the issue; and if so, what you experienced while doing so.

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: We met at the Norwegian's People Aid location, where three, maybe four Mujahedin members came across there. We had a meeting which was very heated. And after quite a long discussion, we managed to settle the disagreement and the Mujahedin would allow the Norwegian's People Aid to have their refugee camp there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Does Arnauti, the location called Arnauti, does it fall within the area of responsibility of the ABiH 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can the witness please be given the Prosecution Exhibit P98. That's the map used earlier on today.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Sir, can you please put it on the ELMO and can you please, if possible, identify on this map the location which you were just talking about and which is called Arnauti.

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes. I'm pointing to it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can the witness please be provided with a text marker.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And, sir, can you please encircle the location which is known as Arnauti.

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Is this the area where the Mujahedin had their camp?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The map can be removed from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Such an event as you just described, sir, with the Mujahedin in Arnauti and the Norwegians complaining about them, would it have been an issue you would have reported at the daily regular 1800 hours' meeting?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I'm now going to show the witness milinfosum number 33 [sic], dated the 5th of June, 1993. We have the necessary copies available in B/C/S and in English. Once the French translations will be available, they will be tendered, if the Trial Chamber allows us to tender the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: I understand -- my case manager is just drawing my attention to the fact that the milinfo number is not correctly reflected in the transcript. It's milinfo number 37 -- sorry -- yes, 37.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Sir, if I may draw your attention to page 3 of this milinfosum, the portion number 10, paragraph number 10. And if you may, please, focus on the section under capital letter B. It says at the beginning "The Zenica LO reports the following," and then there are the capital letters, first A and then B. Sir, are you the Zenica LO, meaning liaison officer, who is referred to in this document?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Sir, have you reported what's written in this document under 10.B?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Is the location which is detailed under 10.B as Arnauti, is this the very same location you just marked at the map Prosecution Exhibit 98?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you, sir, please provide the Trial Chamber with some more information in respect to what it mean that "the Mujahedin have confirmed that they run a training camp in the area of Arnauti."

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: With my discussions with the Mujahedin, that they confirmed that they were running a training camp in that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Does it mean, sir, that you yourself met the Mujahedin who ran the training camp in Arnauti and that you yourself had talked to them?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And what's written in this milinfosum under 10.B, is it the result of what they told you?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Sir, may I in addition draw your attention to the portion under number 5 of the very same milinfosum, number 5, which has the heading "Zenica." My first question, sir: Did Lieutenant Colonel Duncan, did he meet, to your knowledge, with Mr. Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: He met him on many occasions, and obviously the commanding officer, Alastair Duncan, is reporting here in the milinfosum that -- the result of that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Have you, sir, have you been present at such meetings?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: I was present at meetings, but not all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did the commanding officer, Lieutenant Colonel Duncan, report about such meetings at the daily 0800 [sic] hours' meetings in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Were you regularly present when Mr. Duncan reported at such meetings?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did he, to your knowledge, whenever he met with Mr. Hadzihasanovic report about the meeting?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did he report about what has been discussed, addressed at such meetings and what Mr. Hadzihasanovic said at such meetings?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: May I please draw your attention, sir, to the section under 5, which is identified as "comment." This is at the very end of section 5. There it says, and I quote it, that "The BiH were no longer prepared to restrain themselves and were likely to take the military initiative in the Lasva Valley where they enjoy a tactical advantage over the HVO." Sir, based on what you've seen on the ground and of what you got to know talking to the many other people you were referring to earlier on in your today's testimony, based on the reports by Lieutenant Colonel Duncan at the daily 1800 meetings in Vitez, based on this information, would you share the views expressed in this comment?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the Prosecution wishes to tender this milinfosum into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm listening.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. First of all, the first comment regarding the paragraphs that the witness has referred to. We have absolutely no objection on the paragraphs about which he was able to provide information to the Chamber. Under the reservation of the decision taken by the Chamber on a similar document, we have the same objections to make, that the probative value of the other paragraphs will depend on the judgement of the Chamber made subsequently. But I would like to add -- I wanted to do it at the beginning, but I preferred to allow the Prosecution to continue -- and that is that the document such as it is presented to us now is accompanied by a translation into B/C/S. As we mentioned to you earlier on, Mr. President, the Defence is not informed in advance of the documents that will be used through a particular witness. In this case, this translation was never provided to us earlier on, and we were never able to discuss the contents of it with the Prosecution. Mr. President, we hesitate as to what to do in such a situation. What we would like, Mr. President, would be for the Prosecution to indicate to us which document they intend to use in continuation of the examination-in-chief of this witness and the next witness so that we can check that we have the translations in B/C/S, as applies to all the documents on the list that need to be disclosed to the Defence, as covered by the pre-trial brief of the Prosecution, so that we might discuss with the accused the contents of these documents to be able to prepare ourselves properly. Therefore, we do not object to the admission of this document under the reservation of the question of translation, but we would like to Chamber to ask the Prosecution to provide us with the other documents or to inform us of the numbers of the documents that will be used in continuation so that we can check whether we have those documents translated into B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Withopf, regarding this particular point that affects the rights of the accused, we have an official document coming from the British Battalion, and this document and its content is officially stamped, though there is no trace of the stamp. It would appear that these documents communicated to the parties, be it the Prosecution or the Defence, were redacted of other elements, because there should be stamps, et cetera. This is one point which I wish to underline. On the other hand, regarding the rights of the accused, it is necessary for them to be able to judge the translation into their own language and to study the various paragraphs which may contain elements against him. It is true that if a document of several pages is produced at the last moment, the accused is in an inferior position because he doesn't have time to examine the document. He's handicapped by the fact that he cannot read the document in his own language. And though he's assisted by lawyers who have command of English, but that is no reason for the accused not to be able to have their say. As pointed out quite rightly by the Defence counsel, the Chamber is of the opinion that when you plan to tender a document into evidence, because this document which appears on your consolidated list must have been assessed by your side and you knew that you were going to tender it into evidence, and therefore you should have at least informed the Defence of your intention, providing them with a translation of that document so that the Defence might, during the cross-examination, ask appropriate questions. Otherwise, there's disequilibrium. And what has been just said also applies to the Defence, which may have documents in B/C/S which the Prosecution has no command of, and then we will have the same sort of situation. And this remark applies to the Defence. If they intend to tender certain documents they have, they need to have them translated into English so that you can convey your opinion about them. So we have a real problem here which needs to be taken into consideration. I give you the floor, Mr. Withopf --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. President, for a point of clarification. The first document, we didn't receive the translation but we have found a translation of the document of the 5th of June. This is the document which the Prosecution is tendering now. So we did receive a translation. We do not wish to mislead the Chamber. And a very brief adjournment would allow us to discuss with the Prosecution the documents that we have received and which we have not so as to avoid any further problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So the document of the 5th of June, 1993 should have been communicated to the Defence if it was on the consolidated list. And this document should have been accompanied with a B/C/S translation. Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm a bit surprised, to phrase it politely -- I'm a bit surprised about the concerns raised by the Defence. The document milinfosum number 37, dated the 5th of June, 1993 was disclosed in its English original on the 11th of September, 2001 to the Defence, and the B/C/S translation was also disclosed in August 2001 to the Defence. That means Defence and the accused had two and a half years' time to study this document, which is comprised of three pages. I would wish, if Defence in future wishes to tell the Trial Chamber that the Prosecution is not fulfilling its obligations, to first consult the information which is at Defence counsel's disposal and only later on make such observations as has just been made. The Prosecution in anticipating such comments by Defence in this particular -- and in respect to this particular witness has checked, prior to the today's testimony of the witness, whether these documents are on the exhibit list, and the Prosecution would be able to in respect to each and every document it intends to use today to provide the Chamber with the exact date as to when it has been disclosed in English and in B/C/S. Again, I re-emphasise, this document has been disclosed in its B/C/S translation two and a half years ago. The Prosecution reiterates its request that this document be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I shall give the floor to Mr. Bourgon in a minute. But looking at the documents, we see that there's a number, 00273961, on the English text, which is proof that it was communicated to the Defence, and the B/C/S version has another number, 03004069. So we are told that the English document was disclosed to you on the 11th of September, 2001 and the translation earlier, that is, August 2001. So since you knew for a long time now that this witness was going to come and that he belongs to the British Battalion, you should have expected this type of report to be produced in support of the testimony of the witness. So, Mr. Bourgon, are you going to tell me that it's a mistake?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite, Mr. President. It's a mistake that I just told you. I took the floor before my colleague. I told the Chamber that we didn't wish to mislead the Chamber, that we did indeed receive the document of the 5th of June in B/C/S. However, the previous document, dated in May, we did not receive it in B/C/S -- we did not receive the translation of that document. When a witness appears, we do our best to identify the documents which will likely -- are likely to be used. Sometimes we may be mistaken with the documents, but we do our best to find our documents and to check whether we have a translation or not. For the document of the 29th of May, we told the Prosecution that we don't have that translation of that document. We still haven't received it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf, we still have a problem. The document of the 29th of May, which doesn't apparently have a B/C/S translation. Could you tell us something about this document of the 29th of May. Where does the problem lie?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: It may be correct - and I'm about to check it - that this is the only document Defence hasn't received a B/C/S translation. However, in the package Defence was provided with today, the B/C/S translation forms part of. If I may use this opportunity to draw the attention of the Trial Chamber to what happens all the time in this courtroom. Whenever Defence uses a document, Defence doesn't tell the Prosecution prior to using this document. Only in very rare circumstances tells the Prosecution five minutes prior to the court session that they want to use a document and which document they wish to use. In terms of equality of arms, this is certainly the very same situation for both parties. If the Chamber - and I understand the Presiding Judge has already raised this issue - if the Chamber wishes that the parties prior to the court session tell the other party which document they wish to use, that should apply to both parties, meaning that the Defence tells the Prosecution prior to the court session which document they wish to use and provide the Prosecution with an English translation of the document, if the original of this document is only in B/C/S or any other language the Prosecution is not able to understand. The Prosecution so far didn't have a problem - I really wish to emphasise this - with the procedure followed by the Defence, and we have accepted it all the way through of this trial. However, if Defence wishes to get such information days before the witness is called, this procedure should apply vice versa as well. The Prosecution is still prepared to continue on the basis as it has been done in the past. However, if there would be a change, the requirements should apply to the very same extent for both parties. Thank you very much, Mr. President. And again, the Prosecution reiterates its request to tender this milinfosum into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'm finding it a little difficult to follow my colleague. We haven't complained about receiving or not receiving documents. The Prosecution is in a certain position; the Defence in another position; and there really are no problems as far as that is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, we are in open session, and my colleague -- colleague tells the Trial Chamber the names of witnesses. The one or the other of these witnesses, even if they are so-called international witnesses, may have security concerns. I don't think it's appropriate to mention the names of the witnesses in public session. I wish to have this redacted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you prepare an order to have the names mentioned redacted from the transcript, because we don't know whether there will be any requests for protective measures. But this is easy to deal with. However, there are witnesses who will be appearing next week. And apparently the Prosecution hasn't provided the Defence with the translation of their statements into B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, I also don't find it appropriate to mention the names of other witnesses in front of a witness who is in the courtroom. I find it highly problematic. I would recommend if this discussion continues to usher the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. But you want to continue with the discussion about the translations, because the problem isn't witness's names; the problem concerns the translations. We don't necessarily have to refer to Person X, Y, or Z. The problem is there will be witnesses, Witness X, Y, and Z, and their statements in English haven't been translated into B/C/S. Am I right or not? It appears that the Defence doesn't have a number of documents. But this can be dealt with very rapidly.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, what my learned friend from the Defence side hasn't told the Trial Chamber, that these are, in the majority, statements of witnesses whose statements were taken at the very last stages of the investigation, meaning end of last year. The Prosecution does follow the very regular proceedings; namely, request translation immediately after the statement is in, and we are disclosing at the very earliest opportunity once we received the translation. We are working on a daily basis very close together with CLSS to accommodate -- to accommodate the needs of Defence counsel, and we are, as Defence is very well aware of, in almost all instances complying with our legal obligations. In the situations that there are problems, we regularly inform Defence counsel as soon as we get to know, in order to avoid any further problems. And the Prosecution, if I may add this, is taking care of the wishes of Defence. For example, the Prosecution has, for the only reason that Defence didn't have access to the ECMM materials, scheduled the ECMM witnesses towards the very end of this trial in order to enable Defence to properly prepare. The Prosecution does appreciate that the Defence has the right and has the need to timely prepare for the defence and it does everything, each and everything what's possible to accommodate the particular needs of the Defence. Whenever translations are available, they are disclosed immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will give a number to the document dated the 5th of June, 1993. Mr. Registrar, could we have a number for the English and for the B/C/S versions, a final number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the English version gets the number P100; and the B/C/S translation gets the exhibit number P100/BCS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Withopf -- witness, could you make a note of your first and last names on this document and also of today's date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Witness complies]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf may then continue with his examination-in-chief, given that these translation-related issues have resulted in a loss of time. Mr. Withopf, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Sir, during the time you spent in Zenica as a liaison officer for BritBat, did you become aware of situations that members of other international organisations complained about the presence of Mujahedin in the area?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Well, we had the aid organisation, the Norwegian's People Aid, and there may have been other international organisations who have complained when dealing with them. BritBat themselves had occasionally difficulties when they were doing their patrolling.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You earlier on, sir, mentioned that you on a very regular basis and repeatedly had meetings with the 3rd Corps commander, Mr. Enver Hadzihasanovic, in his headquarters in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: With the permission of the Trial Chamber, I'm now going to show the witness a further milinfosum. It's the milinfosum number 055, dated the 23rd of June, 1993. For the information of the Trial Chamber and Defence counsel, the English version has been disclosed on 7th of September, 2001. And according to the information I have at my disposal now, the B/C/S version has been disclosed on 10th of August, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Sir, if I may, please, draw your attention to portion number -- portions number -- paragraphs number 7 and 8, the portions on page 3 with the heading "Zenica." And if I also may draw your attention, sir, in particular to the portion under 8, please. May I please refer to the portion, the very first six lines under paragraph 8. There's a reference made to the following - and I quote - "The Zenica LO also noted that 'Mujahedin' members were seen entering the ops room at 3 Corps headquarters." Sir, are you the Zenica LO referred to in this milinfosum?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you for the benefit of the Trial Chamber confirm today whether what is written in this milinfosum and whether this particular portion is correct, to your recollection.

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes. Because this information I gathered out of -- debriefed the intelligence officer who had compiled this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: If I may draw, sir, your attention to the portion which is following the description "comment." May I draw your particular attention to the following portion, which I'm going to quote now: "This cell believes that they are under effective control as they are invariably found at the point of 3rd Corps main effort. The recent campaign in the Bila Valley clearly demonstrated this." And this portion - that was the end of the quote - this portion is making, as can be seen from the document, is making reference to the Mujahedin. Sir, from what you have seen yourself, from the information you were able to gather, from the daily 1800 hours' meetings in Vitez, based on the information you got from talking to the various people you mentioned today earlier on in your statement, is this statement that I just quoted, is this a statement you would confirm?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes. I think this was -- having collected all the information, the intelligence cell, we had been discussing were they under effective control. And because they were seen as elite troops, they were used to fight the war effectively where they were needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please expand on why they were seen as elite troops.

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: They were seen to be more committed, more determined, more courageous in fighting the war for their fellow Muslim brothers, and therefore it made good military sense to use, you know, the more effective troops where they needed to capture important ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And can you please, sir, for the benefit of the Trial Chamber also explain what you understand under "they were used to fight the war effectively where they were needed."

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: If there was a -- an area of tactical or strategic importance, them being sort of considered better, more elite troops, were obviously used to capture that ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And to your knowledge and what you got to know as a result of the daily meetings and as a result having talked to the variety of people you mentioned earlier on today in your testimony, who was making the decision to have the Mujahedin fighting with the other ABiH units?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Well, this was obviously a decision made by the 3 Corps chain of command to locate their units in their appropriate place.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Sir, if I may draw your attention to a further portion, in paragraph 8, under "comment." And I'm quoting the portion I wish to draw your attention to. It says: "Therefore, the labeling of them" - and "them" is making reference to the Mujahedin - "as uncontrollable becomes a convenient means of deflecting criticism away from 3rd Corps whilst still utilising their proven tactical worth. In this context Hadzihasanovic's letter to his superior command, requesting permission to deal with the problem, might be regarded as rhetoric." May I please draw your attention to this particular portion. Sir, based on what you have seen yourself, based on what you got to know in travelling in the area -- in the wider area of Zenica, based on what you got to know attending -- regularly attending the 1800 hours' meeting each and every day in Vitez, based on what you got to know in talking to the variety of people you mentioned earlier on today during your testimony, would you today, to your recollection, would you confirm this statement?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes. This -- this would confirm what was happening at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. In the course of its cross-examination, the Defence will go into detail to -- but we believe that it might be useful if the Prosecution is ready to do this, it would be useful to know who made these comments. Was it the witness? Was it the intelligence cell? Were they other officers? This is all hearsay. The Trial Chamber has already rendered a decision about hearsay and said that it was necessary to establish the source. Will the source appear as a witness? Will we be provided with additional information, or are we to base ourselves on hearsay alone? Is hearsay the only element that the Prosecution can evoke when a witness appears and then the witness says yes, that's his opinion. It's not just a matter of a witness's opinion, we also need to know the source of hearsay evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, the Prosecution has shown you a document. In paragraph 8 of the document in question, there is a comment in the middle of the paragraph and there is an assessment that is made. So the question is: The comment, which is in fact a conclusion based on a number of factors, whose comment is this? Who made this comment? Did you do so? Did the intelligence officer do it? Did Lieutenant Colonel Duncan make this comment? Or is this a summary of what was said at the table, at the meeting on the 23rd of June? As far as you are concerned, how can you clarify this for us? How can you clarify the conclusion that is presented, the conclusion of a discussion that must have taken place on that day? What can you tell us about this subject?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The comment is written by the intelligence officer, and the word "this cell" is often known as an intelligence cell. So that's where that phrase comes from. The intelligence officer will have compiled the -- the reports that, for instance, I made as liaison officer and combined it with also Colonel Alastair Duncan's meetings and information. So he had the benefit of collating all the information from the different departments within the British Battalion, and he would write the comment. So there, as a result of debriefings he'd received from me, you know, he would also sort of analyse this and sort of put that comment in at the end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as you know, when the report was completed, was it submitted to the lieutenant colonel, to Lieutenant Colonel Duncan, for -- for it to be approved of? Did he read through the final document, or did he not do so? Was it just forwarded further up the chain of command, forwarded to other authorities? Was this document reread and approved by Lieutenant Colonel Duncan? What could you us about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not sure that he always read all of them before they were sent off, but I'm sure there must have been occasions when he read them before they were sent up the chain of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this explanation. Mr. Withopf, we have a few more minutes before our break. But we could have our break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm actually about to finish the examination-in-chief. If you'd allow me five additional minutes, I would finish the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have your five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. Mr. President, Your Honours, the Prosecution wishes to tender milinfosum number 055, dated 23rd of June, 1993 into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Subject to certain provisions, the paragraph which was discussed by the witness and the other paragraphs, so the Defence stands by its objections, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I don't want to trample over old ground, but we are in the same situation again where the comment that was made is not one which was made by -- by this witness. It's recorded in the -- the summary, but the witness has said this is a comment of somebody else. Of course, Your Honour, I understand the distinction between admissibility and probative value; that's the position the Defence has propagated on numerous occasions. But there is also the -- seeking to obtain the best evidence in a trial. The best [Realtime transcript read in error "Bosanski Samac"] evidence rule is a well-known rule in criminal law and international criminal law. And we, in our submission, should guard against introducing a string of hearsay statements and comments when it is quite possible for Your Honours to hear the evidence from the person directly. And that's the only caution I -- I wish to make. In addition to that, Your Honours, the only observation would be that when this witness was asked to comment on this comment, it -- it was a situation where the comment was read out to the witness and he was simply asked to -- to confirm it. Your Honours might think that is one of the more extreme forms of -- of leading a witness. The witness could have been asked what his views were without showing him this document. He made certain observations at the time. He could have been asked to give his opinion without being shown the comment of somebody else who might not even be called as a witness. I'm grateful, Your Honours. Sorry, there is one correction to the transcript. I see "the best evidence rule" was translated as "the Bosanski Samac evidence rule." And I certainly wasn't referring to that as a new rule of evidence on international criminal law. It's the best evidence rule. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, the last issue is certainly an issue both Defence and Prosecution can agree upon. In respect - and I'm referring to the Bosanski Samac rule obviously, to avoid any confusion. In respect to the other comments made my learned friend, it appears to be quite important, and that's the reason why the Prosecution is using the milinfosums. It appears to be quite important to emphasise that the milinfosums, as two witnesses meanwhile have confirmed, were compiled and put together the day of the regular 1800 meetings in Vitez. What's written in the milinfosum reflects the level of information which was compiled by BritBat at the time. The witness has not only commented on the portion that's contained in the milinfosum. The witness has been asked whether he, based on the various sources of information he had at his disposal, is able to confirm, based on his own knowledge - and that was the obvious gist of the question - whether he is able to confirm based on his own knowledge the comments made by somebody else, and the witness has clearly answered this question to the positive. Therefore, this is not an issue of hearsay; this is the witness's own account. Again, the Prosecution reiterates its request to tender this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you have any other questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is the last question to the witness, and the examination-in-chief would be finished once the Trial Chamber has made its decision in respect to tendering this document into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll inform you of our decision a little later. It's twenty-five to 1.00, and we will resume at 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber is rendering its ruling regarding the admission of Exhibit 55 -- or rather, milinfosum 55, dated the 23rd of June, 1993. The Chamber asks the registrar to give it an exhibit number. The Chamber has taken note of the observations made by Mr. Dixon. Clearly this document could also have been introduced when a future witness comes. But as we have a witness who is confirming the elements contained in this document, it is convenient to admit it, though it could be admitted on another occasion. In any event, the probative value will be determined subsequently. Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document will get the exhibit number P101; and the B/C/S translation, the exhibit number P101/BCS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours. As foreshadowed prior to the break, the Prosecution has no further questions at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. We have taken note of that for what you said in particular "for the moment," or "at this point in time." We give the floor now to the Defence for their cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Kiggell.

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm Edina Residovic, and I am Defence counsel for General Enver Hadzihasanovic. In accordance with the Rules and the practice of this Trial Chamber, I will first ask you some general questions regarding the situation about which you're able to testify, on the basis of your knowledge of the facts while you were in the territory of Central Bosnia. I will also have some questions to you linked to today's testimony. If any of my questions is unclear or too comprehensive, please tell me to make myself clearer. Mr. Kiggell, you said that you started your military career in the British Army in 1987; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: To the completion of training in December 1988 in the rank of second lieutenant, you were designated to a platoon commander attached to the Prince of Wales Own Regiment; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In January 1990, you were deployed to Northern Ireland, where you served for about four to five months; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Upon your return from Northern Ireland, you became commander of a military team, a duty that you performed for about 14 months; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Then again in November 1991, you were sent to Northern Ireland again, and you stayed in that position for about half a year; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In answer to a question from my learned friend, you said that you attended a major course, which you completed in December 1992; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After completing this course, you returned to the Prince of Wales Own Battalion, and you were appointed second-in-charge of the company; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: That's correct. It was "C" Company.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In answer to a question from my colleague, you also said that at the beginning of 1993 you were informed that you would be deployed in Bosnia-Herzegovina; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The assignment was part of the peace mission of the United Nations, known as UNPROFOR for short; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In order to prepare for your future assignments and mission, in March 1993 you attended several training courses designed to familiarise you with the situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before that, in view of the work you did in the British Army, you didn't have any specific knowledge about Bosnia and Herzegovina and what was going on there, did you?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: During your training, you were informed about the military situation in the area where you were going on mission, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you arrived in Split, you also received some information regarding the fighting and the locations of those battles, as well as about the forces participating in those battles; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You had particular interest in receiving the information relevant to Central Bosnia, where you were assigned to, and you received that information, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes, we did, and also what was happening in the Tuzla region.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of all these training courses and briefings, at the time you arrived in Bosnia and Herzegovina you knew that Bosnia and Herzegovina was one of the six republics of the former SFRY which in 1992 was granted its independence. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also knew that in May 1992 it was admitted as a member of the United Nations organisation, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: I must have done at the time, yes. I can't remember the exact date.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You probably learnt about the fact that on the day of its recognition Bosnia and Herzegovina was attacked by the Yugoslav army and Serb forces. Were you aware of that fact?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Upon arriving in Bosnia and Herzegovina, though you had significant military experience behind you, nevertheless you didn't have any experience in combat areas, in war-riddled areas; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: No. The operational tours I did in Northern Ireland were to do with terrorists, but not open civil war as was occurring in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: During your trainings, did the information you receive tell you that what was going on in Bosnia and Herzegovina was a civil war?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: I think -- I think the terminology of "civil war," it was a war going on within the different republics within the former Yugoslavia, so my terminology may have not been correct in that last answer I gave you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your clarification. Before coming to Bosnia and Herzegovina, you had never taken part in peace missions of the United Nations, nor did you have any such experience, did you?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You arrived in Bosnia and Herzegovina, as you have already told us, in April; to be specific, on the 28th of April, 1993. And as you already said, you were put up in the old school in Nova Bila, a few kilometres from Vitez; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Before you, the Cheshire Regiment was part of the British forces, and they left the area on the 11th of May, 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact date, but it must have been early May they left.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In any event, you can confirm that for a while, for 7 to 15 days, you were together with your colleagues who were on mission in the area before you.

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: During this joint stay in the area of Central Bosnia, you learnt additional things from your colleagues about the situation in the area of Vitez and the broader area of Central Bosnia; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. I went into Zenica with some of the members of the Cheshire Battalion. And then a few days later, I was also sent up to Tuzla to hand over that region from the departing liaison officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were familiar with the Security Council resolution establishing the mandate of UNPROFOR, which means also the mandate for your own battalion.

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You knew, didn't you, that the previous mandate of UNPROFOR was inadequate and that in September 1992 the Security Council extended the mandate of UNPROFOR, assigning it to protecting land convoys of humanitarian aid organised by UNHCR and also to protect the International Red Cross Committee's work in the exchange of prisoners? Were you aware of this extended mandate of UNPROFOR?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: I can't recall the change, but I certainly remember the role that we had to protect the humanitarian aid convoys and help where was required.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So what I have just said was the mandate given to your mission in Central Bosnia, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Additionally, you were entitled to use arms for self-defence; that is, should you be attacked in performing your duties. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: From early May, from the 1st to the 21st of May, you were on duty in Tuzla, where a part of the BritBat was being set in motion; and then on the 23rd of May, you returned to Vitez again. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: That's about right in time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely during that period the command of your battalion decided to deploy liaison officers in what it considered to be important strategic areas so as to have a clearer idea of what was going on on the ground in the military, social, and political spheres. Was that at the time of your return?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your battalion commander was Lieutenant Colonel Duncan, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel Duncan reviewed this decision and agreed about it with the commander of the 3rd Corps, General Hadzihasanovic, as well as with HVO commanders, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: I think he set the ground for liaison officers to be assigned to various -- the 3 Corps and HVO components. Whether he did it before or after we'd be assigned, I'm not clear on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, the main purpose for establishing liaison officers was to fully implement your mission in terms of free movement of humanitarian aid convoys; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Prior experience made it necessary to envisage potential hot points, and that is why the task of the liaison officer was to prepare as well as he could all the necessary information for the routes for humanitarian aid convoys to be safe and secured prior to the convoys getting on the road; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also had the task of gathering information about the areas of combat or potential areas of combat so that you might better plan the routes to be taken by humanitarian convoys; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: That is correct. We were aimed to get as best a picture of what was going on in our area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So after this decision, on the 21st of May, as you already told us, you were designated the liaison officer for the Zenica region, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: For the British Battalion, Zenica was important, as the command of the 3rd Corps was situated there.

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: It was also significant because routes leading towards Northern and North-Eastern Bosnia passed through Zenica, that is, towards Maglaj, Zavidovici, and Tuzla; would you agree?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Within the framework of the battalion, there were two companies stationed in the area of Vitez; whereas, one company was in Gornji Vakuf, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: That's true. But we also had a company based up in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: These two companies that were based in the area of Vitez, pursuant to the rules of BritBat, would be replaced after a week so that one company secured the command, whereas the other company would be on the ground escorting convoys or investigating the areas. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: They usually changed roles every seven days, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: I think so, yes. I can't remember the exact time period.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The area of responsibility of the 3rd Corps was quite considerable, and it covered the whole of Central Bosnia, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Upon arriving in Zenica, you immediately established contact with the 3rd Corps command, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you have already told us, in answer from questions -- to questions from our learned friends, you carried out your duties by, among other things, meeting in Zenica with representatives of the European monitors and other international non-governmental organisations, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the local level, you would meet with representatives of the civilian and religious life and with ordinary people in the street.

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, as a military man, most frequently you had communications with the 3rd Corps, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You already told my learned friend that regularly, on a daily basis you had meetings in the battalion that were attended by company commanders, liaison officers, intelligence officers, and others; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As a liaison officer, at that meeting you would convey the information you had gathered during the day from various sources, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: That's right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Some of your sources were quite reliable; whereas, others had a lower degree of reliability, and some were quite unreliable. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes, that's true to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the meeting, you would give your own assessment of the knowledge you had gathered that day, but you didn't always necessarily assess the degree of reliability of the sources of your information, did you?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: I would give a summary of the information I had gained and would sometimes pass comment on how reliable it was or not, as the case may be.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Your colleagues acted in a similar manner, the colleagues that were attending that meeting, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes. The liaison officers, if they had gained information from talking to people, would give their assessment on the accuracy of that information.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Some of the information that you conveyed, in view of the degree of reliability, required additional effort for them to be subsequently verified in various other ways; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. We would often perhaps send out another vehicle or call sign, as we would call it, out the following day to verify perhaps movements or where people were located.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As a liaison officer for Zenica, you would give information either to the intelligence officer but most frequently at the regular meetings about the movement of forces, the names of commanders you met or whose names you learnt, and also about locations and any signs of possible conflict along the routes of humanitarian aid convoys; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes. I would debrief the information I'd gained that day to the intelligence officer, who'd write it down. And I'd also give a summary at the 6.00 meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You have already answered that question to some extent, but I would like to ask you once again to tell me whether on the basis of all the information that you gathered a single report was compiled, known as the milinfosum. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And as we were able to see from the milinfosums that were shown to you, these reports contained information provided by a certain person. Then it contained comments by the intelligence officer. And my question to you is: Is it true that it also contained information about meetings that the battalion commander may have had either with representatives of the BH army or with representatives of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes. In the milinfosum, it would say "CO 1 PWO met Enver Hadzihasanovic," for example ^.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If your battalion commander, Lieutenant Colonel Duncan, met in Zenica with Commander Hadzihasanovic, it was customary for you to attend that meeting and to keep notes at that meeting; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: That's right. But I wasn't always present. Sometimes Lieutenant Colonel Duncan and Enver Hadzihasanovic met by themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I should now like to ask you kindly that we go back for a moment to your arrival at the 3rd Corps. You said that during the first few days of your mission you met with the Commander Hadzihasanovic almost daily. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Those meetings took place in his office; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that you believed that the 3rd Corps was in the direction of the Zenica steelworks. If I told you that the 3rd Corps was in fact -- was not in fact located in the direction of the Zenica steelworks but, rather, in a building which located the Institute for Engineering and Planning for that steelwork, you would certainly agree with me.

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This was the project office of the Zenica steelworks; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: It must be, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In view of your answer, you would agree with me that Commander Hadzihasanovic's office wasn't the one used by the director of the Zenica steelworks. It was one of the rooms in this design building. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes. I was trying to give a description earlier on. It was a large office that he used.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If we were able to visualise this office, as my colleague thought that this was an important issue - and I don't want this to remain unclear - one might say that it was a room which was 5 or 5 and a half metres by 3 or 3 and a half metres.

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes, approximately.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: There was the commander's desk in that room. There was a circular table, with 8 seats, 8 chairs for meetings. And there was other furniture for meetings with individual commanders. Is that what one could find in that room?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you have already said, quite frequently or at all times whenever you were there you noticed the commander had military maps on his desk, and you would agree that it is quite normal for a corps commander to have military maps in his office and on his desk, given that this was a commander who was involved in a war. Is that a normal situation?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes, totally normal.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you reported to the 3rd Corps commander as the liaison officer, they made it possible for you to carry out your duties as the liaison officer under normal conditions; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes, that was -- we had very civil conversations and he helped me where possible.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Although you returned to Vitez every day, within the 3rd Corps command you were provided with a room where you could spend time while performing your duties in Zenica in the course of the day; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes. This would be the room where I was assigned a liaison officer, who I think his name was Edo, if I remember correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: We have mentioned Officer Edo again, and I would like to remind you about something and ask you whether this was an intelligence officer who was close to Commander Hadzihasanovic, whose name was Edin Husic ^, also known as Edo. Would that be the person in question?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes, that seems to be the same person.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: It was quite normal, in your opinion, that a corps commander in normal conditions, and especially in wartime conditions, couldn't be at the disposal of the liaison officer from the British Battalion on a daily basis. This was normal for you, and it was understandable. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes, very understandable. He was fighting a war, so I'd speak to somebody within 3 Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, every day, Edin Husic was at your disposal. He was at the disposal of the British Battalion's liaison officer. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes, generally every day he was available.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Whenever you asked Officer Husic to do something, he did all he could in order to provide you with the information you requested; that is to say, to establish the contacts that you wanted to establish. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If there were any problems, problems of any kind that you could not resolve with Officer Husic or if there was a problem that was outside the scope of your responsibilities, then there would be meetings between Colonel Duncan and Commander Hadzihasanovic; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And this was also quite normal, in your opinion. The battalion commander should have communication with the corps commander, that would be the normal route of establishing such contact. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes, it would be quite normal for my commanding officer also to have a direct relationship with the commander of 3 Corps.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that on a number of occasions you also met the deputy corps commander, Dzemal Merdan; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Dzemal Merdan, just like Commander Hadzihasanovic and Officer Husic, attempted to answer all the questions that you had and to find the best way that would enable you to successfully carry out the mission that you had been assigned as the liaison officer; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes, generally that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When performing that mandate, up until the 31st of August, 1993, you can confirm that there was not a single situation in the area under the control of the BH army in which there were problems or in which humanitarian aid convoys were stopped. And this was your main and primary task. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: There were sometimes occasions of problems of transit through a checkpoint, which we would then have to go to 3 Corps to get permission to get through. And sometimes this would delay the whole convoy, and sometimes we may not be able to do it for that day, we'd have to do it for a second day. So we'd have to get a piece of paper signed by either Hadzihasanovic, Merdan, or someone from 3 Corps to let us go that checkpoint, to let the convoy go through.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, you would agree with me if I said that although there were perhaps slight delays, all the humanitarian aid convoys escorted by the UNHCR or by other international organisations that you assisted managed to pass through the areas under the control of the 3rd Corps without any problems, or rather, they managed to pass through the areas where you were located. That is to say, they passed through Zenica without any problems.

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes, part -- I would agree with that. They passed through Zenica without any problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, in the course of the testimony you have given here today, you said that on occasion it was difficult for you to pass through a checkpoint and on such occasions you had to receive permission to pass through. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also said that such permission was usually given to you by Dzemal Merdan; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes. I think sometimes people would ask, you know, for Hadzihasanovic's signature. We had to get so many pieces of paper. I can't remember who -- you know, how many signed each at each time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: On the main road used by the humanitarian aid convoys, there were no such problems. Or if there were any such problems, they were very slight. I'm referring to the main routes used by the humanitarian convoys. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In fact, the problems first started appearing when your vehicles or you personally or some of the convoys entered areas which were closer to the confrontation lines; is that right?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: That may have occurred. There was one occasion where Merdan had complained to me where a British Army vehicle, a Warrior, had -- was at a key point for the BiH forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And similarly, if such locations were close to the confrontation lines or areas where there was open fighting, this could pose a risk for the safety of UNPROFOR; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: Possibly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So it was quite normal for a commander to first draw your attention to this fact or to request that the fighting cease before you entered a given area with your forces, and it was normal for him to do so in order to ensure your safety; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: CAMERON KIGGELL
utterances.text: There would have been occasions where we asked for -- you know, for a safe transit of either UNPROFOR or the aid organisations through an area, so we would organise a cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, given that I'll now be moving on to another area that I would like to question the witness about and it is now quarter to 2.00, perhaps this might be the right time to -- to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Withopf, the witness will unfortunately have to return tomorrow. He was here yesterday too. But there is nothing else to be done, since the cross-examination must be continued. So, Witness, please come back tomorrow morning and I think that by the end of the morning you will be able to leave. I'll now ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom, and I will see you tomorrow. Madam Usher, please escort the witness out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
